fields.Text: The network core is a {{c1::mesh of interconnected routers}} that forwards packets from router to router along the path from source to destination.
In packet switching each packet is transmitted at the {{c1::full link capacity (transmission rate R)}} of the link, not a fraction of it.

fields.Back: The entire packet must arrive at a router (be stored) before its first bit can be transmitted on the next link.

fields.Text: Store-and-forward: the {{c1::entire packet}} must arrive at the router before it can be transmitted on the next link; end-to-end delay over one router (two links) is {{c2::2L/R}} ignoring propagation.
Transmission delay of an L-bit packet on a link of rate R: d_trans = {{c1::L / R}} seconds.
fields.Extra: Bits divided by bits per second.

fields.Text: Slide example: L = 10 Kbits, R = 100 Mbps gives a one-hop transmission delay of {{c1::0.1 ms}}.
One packet over N links each of rate R, store-and-forward, no propagation/processing delay: end-to-end delay = {{c1::N * L / R}}.

fields.Front: Numeric: a 5,000-bit packet crosses 3 links of 2 Mbps each (2 routers), no propagation/processing delay. End-to-end delay?
Sending P packets over N links (each rate R) with store-and-forward takes how long?
fields.Back: (N + P - 1) * L / R, because transmissions pipeline: the source sends packet 2 while the router forwards packet 1. E.g., 3 packets over 2 links = 4L/R.

fields.Front: When do packets queue at a router, and when are they lost?
fields.Back: They queue when the arrival rate (bps) to a link exceeds the link's transmission rate for a period of time; they are dropped (lost) when the router's buffer memory fills up.
A LOCAL action: moving an arriving packet from the router's input link to the appropriate output link, by looking up the destination address in the packet header in the local forwarding table.
A GLOBAL action: determining the source-to-destination paths taken by packets, performed by routing algorithms; the results populate each router's local forwarding table.

fields.Text: Forwarding is a {{c1::local}} action (input link to output link using the forwarding table); routing is a {{c2::global}} action (determining source-destination paths via routing algorithms).
